contributions.statement: When an agent is asked to fix a Java performance issue, require a JMH benchmark or a warmed, repeated-timing detector test with a statistical threshold as the acceptance oracle, because existing JUnit suites showed a significant speedup for only 19 of 102 real performance patches (8 under a conservative threshold) and wrong patches still pass them.
contributions.evidence: §5.1 and §6.1: 19/102 ETIPs have any test class with significant improvement (6 of them also show a regression); JMH present in only 14/91 projects; §5.2 notes incorrect patches pass existing tests. Audit grades the 'tests lack' inference moderate (class-level timing is noisy).
relative_to: functional tests do not verify non-functional properties (2608.26391)

contributions.statement: Expect an off-the-shelf agent (OpenHands with GPT-5-mini) to correctly fix only about 1 in 7 real Maven performance issues, with multi-module changes the weakest case, so performance work should not be delegated without a human-owned benchmark.
contributions.evidence: §5.2 Table 3: 13/91 correct (judged by similarity to ground truth, one author, one run); 36-62% of runs emit no patch; 2 multi-module successes. Audit: 14.3% is 3-5x higher than OpenHands on GSO/PerfBench, suggesting contamination or easier tasks.

reason: The Java-specific finding that existing JUnit suites almost never demonstrate a speedup gives a concrete acceptance-oracle rule for performance specs. The fix-rate number is weak (manual similarity judging, contamination risk).
